title: Living in a high-rise flat with arthritis and frailty (UK)
meta_title: High-Rise Flats, Arthritis and Frailty: Lifts and Getting Out
meta_description: Practical tips for living in an upstairs or high-rise flat with arthritis and frailty: broken lifts, stairs, deliveries, fire safety and getting help.

direct_answer: If you live in a high-rise flat with arthritis and frailty, plan for lift breakdowns, tell your landlord about your needs, use deliveries for heavy shopping, and make sure your landlord knows you may need help in an evacuation. If stairs are no longer safe, ask about rehousing or adaptations.

content:
Living in an upstairs or high-rise flat can work well, but when arthritis and frailty make stairs difficult, a broken lift can leave you stuck at home or unable to get back in. Planning ahead can reduce the risk.

This guide covers lifts, stairs, deliveries, fire safety and housing options. It is educational information, not legal advice.

When the lift breaks down

  • Report breakdowns to your landlord or managing agent promptly, and tell them if you cannot use the stairs.
  • Ask if they keep a list of residents who need extra help.
  • Keep a few days of food and medicines in reserve.
  • Have neighbours' and family numbers ready so someone can help with shopping.

Making the stairs safer

  • Use handrails on both sides if available; ask your landlord about adding a second rail.
  • Rest on landings and take your time.
  • Carry less: use deliveries and a shoulder or cross-body bag to keep a hand free.
  • Ask a physiotherapist about stair technique: up with the stronger leg first, down with the more painful leg first.

Fire safety

Tell your landlord if you would have difficulty leaving the building in an emergency. In England, landlords of high-rise residential buildings have duties to plan for residents who need help to evacuate. Your local fire and rescue service may offer a free home fire safety visit.

Getting shopping and medicines

  • Use online grocery deliveries and ask for delivery to your door.
  • Ask your pharmacy about prescription delivery.
  • Community volunteers and good neighbour schemes may help.

Housing options

If stairs or lifts are making life unsafe, talk to your landlord or council about a move to a ground-floor or adapted property. Medical evidence from your GP or occupational therapist can support an application.

When to get help

  • Call 999 for chest pain, trouble breathing, signs of a stroke, or a fall with a possible serious injury.
  • Get urgent advice the same day (NHS 111 or your GP) for sudden confusion, a sudden drop in mobility, or a hot, swollen joint with fever.
  • See your GP for a steady decline over weeks, unplanned weight loss or repeated falls.

Never stop or change a prescribed medicine yourself. Ask your GP or pharmacist for a review.

Common questions

Can my landlord refuse to fix the lift?

Landlords are usually responsible for maintaining lifts in shared areas. Contact Shelter, Citizens Advice or your local advice service if repairs are delayed.

Is a ground-floor flat always better?

Often, but think about access, security and being near shops and transport.

What if I fall on the stairs?

A community alarm can call for help. Call 999 if you may be seriously hurt.
